Reference: Duflo et al. (2018)

Model Setting

The paper asks whether regulatory discretion helps or hurts the enforcement of pollution standards. The setting is Gujarat, India, where the Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB) regulates about 20,000 industrial plants under strict emission limits. Penalties are severe when applied (in 2008 the GPCB ordered 9% of sample plants to close, at least temporarily, sometimes by cutting off water and electricity), but the chance of being caught is low: the regulator has a limited inspection budget and chooses which plants to inspect, so half of plants are inspected less often than the prescribed rate while similar plants are inspected many times more. Discretion would hurt if plants bribe to avoid inspections or the regulator shirks; it would help if the regulator uses local information to target the dirtiest plants.

The paper combines a two-year field experiment on 960 plants with a structural model. The experimental treatment bundled two changes: more inspection resources, and the removal of discretion over the extra inspections, which were assigned at random. Because the treatment changes both at once, the model is needed to separate the value of resources from the value of discretion. The model has two stages. In the targeting stage, a benevolent regulator chooses an inspection rule, based on plant observables and a noisy signal of pollution, to maximize abatement subject to an inspection budget; plants decide whether to run their abatement equipment given the inspection threat. In the penalty stage, after an initial inspection, a regulatory machine follows fixed rules for followup and punishment, and plants solve a single-agent dynamic problem of when to comply. The penalty stage delivers the value to a plant of being inspected at a given pollution level, which drives abatement incentives in the targeting stage. The model abstracts from corruption in the assignment of inspections (bribes during inspections are allowed).

Experimental Design and Data

From a population of 3455 red-category (high pollution potential) small and medium plants in Ahmedabad, Surat and Valsad, the authors drew 960 plants: all 473 audit-eligible plants in Ahmedabad and Surat and 488 randomly chosen audit-ineligible plants. Between August 2009 and May 2011, the 481 treatment plants were assigned at least one annual initial inspection and up to four per year: one in the first quarter, then a new inspection each quarter with probability 0.66. Each morning inspection teams received a random list of treatment plants. Treatment and control inspection reports entered the same database without a flag, were analyzed by the same labs, and were followed up by the same officials. The regulator kept discretion over its existing inspection budget in both arms. Data come from an independent end-line survey (April to July 2011) of pollution and abatement costs, and from 9624 GPCB documents that the authors code into actions of the regulator (inspect, warn, punish, accept) and the plant (comply, ignore), linked into chains of interactions. In these chains 87% end after a single inspection, with the regulator accepting in the third round.

Experimental Evidence

The treatment was implemented: control plants were inspected 1.40 times per year, and treatment plants an additional 1.71 times (3.11 in total), with initial inspections up by 1.50 per year. Treatment plants were 0.21 more likely to have a pollution reading collected (control base 0.38), 0.22 more likely to be found above a standard, and received more citations (0.20) and closure warnings (0.077). But costly penalties (closure directions, equipment mandates, utility disconnections) did not rise significantly. The treatment reduced end-line pollution by 0.105 standard deviations (standard error 0.084), insignificant, and raised compliance by 3.7 percentage points (standard error 2.1) on a base of 61%, with mass shifting from just above to just below the standard. Maintenance spending rose by 838 dollars (standard error 499).

Three facts point to status quo targeting. First, the treatment cut the share of plants inspected below the prescribed rate from 50% to 13% but did not raise the number of plants with five or more inspections. Second, it did not find more extreme violators: 35 (10) treatment plants had a reading above five (ten) times the standard against 33 (12) in the control. Third, control-group end-line readings, which the regulator never saw, predict future inspections conditional on observables and past readings, so the regulator has its own pollution signals. Random inspections mostly found modest violators whom the regulator would not have punished anyway.

Steep targeting puts inspections where expected penalties and abatement quantities are largest; flat targeting catches plants with low running costs. Targeting Stage Estimation (GMM)

The targeting stage is a system of equations for inspections, pollution and the run decision, where the run decision is endogenous to shocks unobserved by the econometrician. The parameters θT={ϕ,β,λ1,λ2,μc,σ1,σ2}\theta_T=\{\phi,\beta,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_c,\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}θT​={ϕ,β,λ1​,λ2​,μc​,σ1​,σ2​} are estimated by GMM with analytic and simulated moments, using the cross section of initial inspections per year IjI_jIj​, characteristics XjX_jXj​, treatment TjT_jTj​, end-line pollution PjP_jPj​ (the maximum over pollutants of the log reading in units of the standard) and cj×runc_j\times runcj​×run. Two parameters are fixed: σc=0.5\sigma_c=0.5σc​=0.5 (roughly the midpoint of imprecise estimates from higher-order moments of the truncated cost distribution, since only about 10% of plants run) and ρ=0.25\rho=0.25ρ=0.25 standard deviations of observed pollution (close to a pure scale factor that β,λ\beta,\lambdaβ,λ can offset). With Zj=[1,Xj,Tj]Z_j=[\mathbf{1},X_j,T_j]Zj​=[1,Xj​,Tj​], the first set of moments uses the pollution equation error, orthogonal to treatment:

Imposing Optimal Targeting

In the constrained estimation, the minimization is subject to the first-order conditions of the regulator's Lagrangian. Writing A(λ)\mathcal{A}(\lambda)A(λ) for the objective in the regulator's problem, B(λ)\mathcal{B}(\lambda)B(λ) for the left side of the budget constraint and η\etaη for its multiplier, these conditions require the marginal abatement from each targeting parameter to equal its marginal use of the budget:

∂A(λ)∂λℓ=η ∂B(λ)∂λℓ,ℓ=1,2,B(λ)=N⋅Iˉ(9.3.1.21)\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_\ell}=\eta\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_\ell},\quad \ell=1,2,\qquad \mathcal{B}(\lambda)=N\cdot\bar{I} \tag{9.3.1.21}∂λℓ​∂A(λ)​=η∂λℓ​∂B(λ)​,ℓ=1,2,B(λ)=N⋅Iˉ(9.3.1.21)

Under the probit form the three conditions impose two independent nonlinear constraints. Optimality is tested by a distance metric test: the sample size times the difference between the constrained and unconstrained minimized criteria is distributed χ22\chi_2^2χ22​ under the null.

Identification and Sensitivity

The experiment is the key source of identification. Using the Andrews, Gentzkow and Shapiro (2017) sensitivity measure, the targeting parameters are most sensitive to the products of treatment with inspections and inspections squared: if treated plants' mean inspections rose from 2.93 to 3.93 per year, λ^2\hat{\lambda}_2λ^2​ would rise from 10.06 to 26.23 and λ^1\hat{\lambda}_1λ^1​ fall from −0.22-0.22−0.22 to −0.58-0.58−0.58 (if treatment raised inspections a lot, the status quo rule must have been steep). Information σ12/(σ12+σ22)\sigma_1^2/(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)σ12​/(σ12​+σ22​) depends on the dispersion of inspections and their covariance with pollution: a one standard deviation rise in mean inspections squared (7.53 to 17.12) would raise it by about 0.31 from a base of 0.02. Abatement efficacy ϕ^2\hat{\phi}_2ϕ^​2​ depends on the pollution residual in the treatment group (one standard deviation more treatment pollution moves it from −0.71-0.71−0.71 to −0.51-0.51−0.51) and on costs (a 100 dollar rise in mean maintenance cost among runners moves it to −0.53-0.53−0.53). These sensitivities refer to the unconstrained estimates. Moving σc\sigma_cσc​ from 0.25 to 1.00 moves ϕ^2\hat{\phi}_2ϕ^​2​ from −0.60-0.60−0.60 to −1.07-1.07−1.07, both within one standard deviation of the baseline.

Penalty Stage Estimates

The machine is much more likely to punish after high readings (punish coefficient 1.15 for 5+ times the standard) and less likely to warn or punish after prior warnings or plant compliance. In the penalty estimates (in thousands of dollars, 1474 plant moves), a constant punishment costs a plant τ^0=53.54\hat{\tau}_0=53.54τ^0​=53.54 (standard error 24.68). Letting the penalty vary with pollution gives τ^1=39.57\hat{\tau}_1=39.57τ^1​=39.57, τ^2=54.11\hat{\tau}_2=54.11τ^2​=54.11 and τ^3=41.51\hat{\tau}_3=41.51τ^3​=41.51, and flatness cannot be rejected. When inspections are also costly, the punishment cost falls to τ^0=28.12\hat{\tau}_0=28.12τ^0​=28.12 (standard error 20.88) with a per-inspection cost ν^0=9.67\hat{\nu}_0=9.67ν^0​=9.67 (3.07). With pollution-varying inspection costs, τ^0=36.71\hat{\tau}_0=36.71τ^0​=36.71 and ν^1,ν^2,ν^3=10.93,9.72,5.83\hat{\nu}_1,\hat{\nu}_2,\hat{\nu}_3=10.93,9.72,5.83ν^1​,ν^2​,ν^3​=10.93,9.72,5.83, so inspections cost one-third or less of punishment. The shock scale σ^a\hat{\sigma}_aσ^a​ is between 4.83 and 5.88 across specifications. A punishment of about 54,000 dollars is more than three times the mean equipment cost, and it matches lost profits from a median 24.5-day closure if variable margins are 20–30%. At the first plant move (t=2t=2t=2), the value of regulation ranges from −1160-1160−1160 dollars with no reading to −6240-6240−6240 dollars for a reading above five times the standard. Averaged over the first-inspection pollution distribution it is −2131-2131−2131 dollars, 40% from penalties and 60% from abatement capital. Penalties are costly but rare.

Targeting Stage Estimates

In the constrained model, treatment raises the targeting index by 0.095 (about two extra inspections per year at the margin), and running equipment lowers log pollution by ϕ^2=−1.902\hat{\phi}_2=-1.902ϕ^​2​=−1.902 (0.160), an 85% reduction, in line with engineering efficacies of air pollution control devices. The regulator sees little: σ^1=0.069\hat{\sigma}_1=0.069σ^1​=0.069 (0.003) against σ^2=1.033\hat{\sigma}_2=1.033σ^2​=1.033 (0.047), so less than 1% of pollution variance is observable. Yet it targets aggressively: λ^2=33.02\hat{\lambda}_2=33.02λ^2​=33.02 and λ^1=−0.395\hat{\lambda}_1=-0.395λ^1​=−0.395. An audit-eligible control plant in Ahmedabad expects 0.56 inspections at the 5th percentile of the observed shock and 3.48 at the 95th; half of plants get fewer than one inspection a year while the plants expected to be dirtiest may get ten. The mean log maintenance cost is μ^c=2.388\hat{\mu}_c=2.388μ^​c​=2.388. Without the optimality constraints, targeting is somewhat flatter (λ^2=10.06\hat{\lambda}_2=10.06λ^2​=10.06, λ^1=−0.220\hat{\lambda}_1=-0.220λ^1​=−0.220), the observed share is larger (σ^1=0.111\hat{\sigma}_1=0.111σ^1​=0.111, σ^2=0.864\hat{\sigma}_2=0.864σ^2​=0.864), and abatement is less effective (ϕ^2=−0.711\hat{\phi}_2=-0.711ϕ^​2​=−0.711, standard error 0.308). Very aggressive targeting is optimal only when abatement is large. The distance metric test rejects optimality (χ22=16.10\chi_2^2=16.10χ22​=16.10, p-value 0.0003), but the constrained and unconstrained rules lie nearly on top of each other except at the highest signals. The model fits the inspection distributions by arm and the pollution distribution, and it reproduces the experimental shift of mass from just above to just below the standard.

Counterfactuals: The Value of Discretion

Holding the penalty stage fixed (a medium-run exercise), the paper solves the regulator's problem for different budgets Iˉ\bar{I}Iˉ under four regimes: (1) a uniform rule giving every plant the same inspections (no information); (2) optimal discretionary targeting on the observed shock u1ju_{1j}u1j​; (3) discretionary targeting with full information, σ2=0\sigma_2=0σ2​=0, feasible with continuous emissions monitoring systems (CEMS); (4) a hybrid like the experiment, with the first 1.47 inspections (control mean) allocated with discretion and extra ones uniformly. The results are as follows.

(i) A uniform rule does very poorly at low budgets. At about 1.5 inspections per plant, mean abatement is only 0.06, since few plants have trivial maintenance costs and thin inspections leave preemptive abatement unprofitable.

(ii) Discretion triples abatement at the status quo budget (0.17 against 0.06); a uniform rule would need about 2.2 inspections per plant to match it. The value of discretion is largest at tight budgets.

(iii) The experimental hybrid adds about 1.5 random inspections and raises abatement by 0.14 standard deviations, because plants not targeted by the regulator get too few random inspections to abate. Allocating the same extra inspections with discretion would have raised abatement about 15% more (0.16), an arc elasticity of pollution with respect to discretionary inspections of −0.27-0.27−0.27.

(iv) Better information raises abatement by 30% on average across budgets, with the gain increasing in the budget. At the control budget it is worth about as much as a one-third larger budget allocated with discretion. CEMS for particulate matter cost about 1800 dollars per plant-year, against 70 dollars for one in-person inspection with sampling.

The overall lesson is that removing discretion would undercut enforcement even with weak institutions, extra resources alone help modestly, and poor information is a binding constraint.

This is the data-generating assumption for latent pollution, the pollution plant jjj would emit in period mmm if it did not run its abatement equipment. The left side is in logs, so every term on the right shifts pollution proportionally. ϕ0\phi_0ϕ0​ is an intercept, ϕ1Xj\phi_1X_jϕ1​Xj​ is the part predicted by observables (sector, size, region, audit eligibility), and the residual is split into two pieces with very different informational roles. u1ju_{1j}u1j​ is a permanent plant shock that both the plant and the regulator see; it has no period index, so it is the stable component of dirtiness that a regulator can learn from past visits or local knowledge. u2jmu_{2jm}u2jm​ is redrawn every period and is seen only by the plant. The econometrician sees neither.

The additive split is what lets the paper define the regulator's information as a variance share, equation (3), and what makes the targeting rule in equation (9) a function of u1ju_{1j}u1j​ alone. In levels the equation reads

P~jm=exp⁡(ϕ0+ϕ1Xj)⋅eu1j⋅eu2jm\tilde{P}_{jm}=\exp(\phi_0+\phi_1X_j)\cdot e^{u_{1j}}\cdot e^{u_{2jm}}P~jm​=exp(ϕ0​+ϕ1​Xj​)⋅eu1j​⋅eu2jm​

so the regulator knows latent pollution up to the multiplicative factor eu2jme^{u_{2jm}}eu2jm​. Given what it sees, its forecast of log latent pollution is ϕ0+ϕ1Xj+u1j\phi_0+\phi_1X_j+u_{1j}ϕ0​+ϕ1​Xj​+u1j​, with forecast error variance σ22\sigma_2^2σ22​. Latent pollution is never observed directly: the data contain PjmP_{jm}Pjm​ after the run decision, equation (4), which is why the coefficients ϕ\phiϕ are estimated from the moment in equation (17) rather than by regressing on equation (1).

These are the distributional assumptions that close the targeting stage. Both pollution shocks are mean-zero normals, so latent pollution in equation (1) is lognormal conditional on XjX_jXj​, with residual log variance σ12+σ22\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2σ12​+σ22​. The mean-zero normalization is harmless because ϕ0\phi_0ϕ0​ absorbs the means. The cost cjc_jcj​ of operating and maintaining abatement equipment for the period is lognormal: it is strictly positive, right-skewed, and has

The objective is in pollution levels, not logs, so abatement at very dirty plants is weighted heavily; and it counts only abatement from the run decision, ignoring any value of the penalty stage itself.

which shows the trade-off inside the budget: raising the cap λ2\lambda_2λ2​ must be paid for by lowering the shifter λ1\lambda_1λ1​.

This is the assumed parametric family for the targeting rule: annual initial inspections are a scaled normal CDF of an index that is linear in observables, treatment, and the shock the regulator sees. λ2>0\lambda_2>0λ2​>0 is the maximum number of inspections any plant can receive; λ1\lambda_1λ1​ shifts the index and so sets how many plants sit near zero or near the cap; β1\beta_1β1​ loads on plant characteristics; β2\beta_2β2​ is the shift from treatment assignment, which is how the experiment's extra inspections enter; ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0 scales the index and is fixed at 0.25 standard deviations of observed pollution. The u1u_1u1​ inside is the plant's observed shock u1ju_{1j}u1j​ (the plant subscript is dropped in the note and in the paper). The rule is bounded and increasing in the observed shock:

0<I<λ2,∂I∂u1=λ2ρ φ(λ1+Xj′β1+Tj′β2+u1ρ)>00<\mathcal{I}<\lambda_2,\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{I}}{\partial u_1}=\frac{\lambda_2}{\rho}\,\varphi\left(\frac{\lambda_1+X_j'\beta_1+T_j'\beta_2+u_1}{\rho}\right)>00<I<λ2​,∂u1​∂I​=ρλ2​​φ(ρλ1​+Xj′​β1​+Tj′​β2​+u1​​)>0

where φ\varphiφ is the standard normal density. The slope is steepest, λ2φ(0)/ρ\lambda_2\varphi(0)/\rhoλ2​φ(0)/ρ, where the index is zero. Because u1u_1u1​ enters with a unit coefficient and has standard deviation σ1\sigma_1σ1​, a small ρ\rhoρ relative to σ1\sigma_1σ1​ approaches a threshold rule (inspect λ2\lambda_2λ2​ times if the index is positive, never otherwise), and a large ρ\rhoρ approaches a uniform rule. A high λ2\lambda_2λ2​ with a very negative λ1\lambda_1λ1​ puts almost every plant in the lower tail and concentrates inspections on the few observed to be dirtiest.

The form is restrictive, since an unconstrained regulator need not choose from this family, but it spans uniform to very steep rules with two free parameters (λ1,λ2)(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)(λ1​,λ2​), which is what makes the optimality conditions in equation (21) tractable. It also yields analytic moments: the mean and mean square of inspections in equations (18) and (19) and the budget in equation (8).

This is the policy function of the regulatory machine: the probability that the regulator takes action aaa in its next move, given the state st+1s_{t+1}st+1​ reached after the plant's move. It is a multinomial logit over the four actions inspect, warn, punish and accept. The state vector contains indicators for lagged warn, punish and comply, pollution-reading bins (0–1, 1–2, 2–5 and 5+ times the standard, with no reading omitted) and round dummies. Each non-base action has its own coefficient vector γa\gamma_aγa​; accept is the base, γaccept=0\gamma_{\text{accept}}=0γaccept​=0, which is needed because only differences in the indices are identified. The coefficients are log odds relative to accept:

log⁡Pr⁡(aR,t+1=a∣st+1)Pr⁡(aR,t+1=accept∣st+1)=st+1′γa\log\frac{\Pr(a_{R,t+1}=a\mid s_{t+1})}{\Pr(a_{R,t+1}=\text{accept}\mid s_{t+1})}=s_{t+1}'\gamma_alogPr(aR,t+1​=accept∣st+1​)Pr(aR,t+1​=a∣st+1​)​=st+1′​γa​

For example, the punish coefficient of 1.15 on the bin for readings above five times the standard multiplies the odds of punish relative to accept by e1.15≈3.2e^{1.15}\approx 3.2e1.15≈3.2 compared with a chain without a reading.

This equation is a reduced-form description of behavior, not the solution to an optimization problem: the machine is not a strategic player, and the logit is estimated directly from the observed chains of regulator actions. The plant knows these probabilities, and they enter its dynamic problem as the weights Pr⁡(aR,t+1∣st+1)\Pr(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})Pr(aR,t+1​∣st+1​) in equation (13). The policy is held fixed in counterfactuals, so the counterfactuals change who gets inspected, not what happens after an inspection.

This is the plant's within-round payoff when the machine chooses punish, in the specification where the penalty varies with pollution. The parameters τ1,τ2,τ3\tau_1,\tau_2,\tau_3τ1​,τ2​,τ3​ are costs in dollars (positive values mean losses, hence the minus signs) for readings in three bins defined relative to the legal standard pˉ\bar{p}pˉ​: between one and two times, between two and five times, and five times or more. Exactly one indicator is on for a reading above the standard. For a reading at or below the standard, or when no reading was taken, all indicators are zero and h=0h=0h=0. That zero is not an estimate but a normalization: together with the zero payoff of ignore it supplies the two known payoffs needed for identification of the dynamic discrete choice model. The simpler specification replaces the step function with a constant h(pjt)=−τ0h(p_{jt})=-\tau_0h(pjt​)=−τ0​.

The parameters are not read from fines or statutes. They are recovered by revealed preference: τ\tauτ enters πj(aR,t+1∣st+1)\pi_j(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})πj​(aR,t+1​∣st+1​) in equation (13) when the machine punishes, and it is identified by how willing plants are to pay the known compliance cost kkk of 17,000 dollars in states where the machine, by equation (10), is likely to punish. The step function allows a test of whether dirtier plants face harsher punishment. The estimates (in thousand dollars) are τ^1=39.57\hat{\tau}_1=39.57τ^1​=39.57, τ^2=54.11\hat{\tau}_2=54.11τ^2​=54.11, τ^3=41.51\hat{\tau}_3=41.51τ^3​=41.51, which are not monotone and not statistically different from the constant τ^0=53.54\hat{\tau}_0=53.54τ^0​=53.54. Higher pollution still raises expected penalties, but through a higher probability of punishment in equation (10), not a larger penalty when punished.

This is the cost a plant bears when it is inspected in the penalty stage, covering disruption of production, management time, and side payments (hence the shorthand bribes). It is a cost: with ν>0\nu>0ν>0 it enters the plant's within-round payoff with a negative sign, πj(inspect∣st)=−b(pjt,aj−)\pi_j(\text{inspect}|s_t)=-b(p_{jt},a_{j-})πj​(inspect∣st​)=−b(pjt​,aj−​). The first factor switches the cost off for a plant whose recent action aj−a_{j-}aj−​ was comply. The second factor lets the cost depend on the reading through the same three bins relative to the standard pˉ\bar{p}pˉ​ as in equation (11). Written by cases,

b(pjt,aj−)={0if aj−=Comply, or pjt≤pˉ, or no readingν1if aj−≠Comply and pˉ<pjt<2pˉν2if aj−≠Comply and 2pˉ≤pjt<5pˉν3if aj−≠Comply and 5pˉ≤pjtb(p_{jt},a_{j-})=\begin{cases}0 & \text{if } a_{j-}=\text{Comply, or } p_{jt}\le\bar{p}\text{, or no reading}\\ \nu_1 & \text{if } a_{j-}\ne\text{Comply and } \bar{p}<p_{jt}<2\bar{p}\\ \nu_2 & \text{if } a_{j-}\ne\text{Comply and } 2\bar{p}\le p_{jt}<5\bar{p}\\ \nu_3 & \text{if } a_{j-}\ne\text{Comply and } 5\bar{p}\le p_{jt}\end{cases}b(pjt​,aj−​)=⎩⎨⎧​0ν1​ν2​ν3​​if aj−​=Comply, or pjt​≤pˉ​, or no readingif aj−​=Comply and pˉ​<pjt​<2pˉ​if aj−​=Comply and 2pˉ​≤pjt​<5pˉ​if aj−​=Comply and 5pˉ​≤pjt​​

In the constant specification the bracket is replaced by a single ν0\nu_0ν0​.

The economic idea is that an inspector has leverage only over a plant that is in violation and has not yet fixed the problem. Including bbb changes the interpretation of the other estimates: if inspections are themselves costly, less of the observed compliance has to be rationalized by punishment, so τ^0\hat{\tau}_0τ^0​ falls from 53.54 to 28.12 thousand dollars when ν^0=9.67\hat{\nu}_0=9.67ν^0​=9.67 is added. The ν\nuν parameters are identified separately from τ\tauτ because equation (10) makes inspect and punish likely in different states, and because compliance removes bbb but not necessarily the threat of punishment. The cost enters the plant's problem through πj(aR,t+1∣st+1)\pi_j(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})πj​(aR,t+1​∣st+1​) in equation (13).

The plant moves in even rounds and the machine in odd rounds, so between two plant decisions (rounds ttt and t+2t+2t+2) the machine moves once (round t+1t+1t+1). Start from the generic Bellman principle: the value of choosing ajta_{jt}ajt​ in state sts_tst​ is the current payoff, including the action-specific shock, plus the discounted expected value of everything that follows,

vj(ajt∣st)=πj(ajt∣st)+ej(ajt∣st)+δ∑st+1f(st+1∣ajt,st) W(st+1)v_j(a_{jt}|s_t)=\pi_j(a_{jt}|s_t)+e_j(a_{jt}|s_t)+\delta\sum_{s_{t+1}}f(s_{t+1}|a_{jt},s_t)\,W(s_{t+1})vj​(ajt​∣st​)=πj​(ajt​∣st​)+ej​(ajt​∣st​)+δst+1​∑​f(st+1​∣ajt​,st​)W(st+1​)

At that node the plant makes no choice. It receives the payoff that the machine's action imposes on it (zero for warn and accept, h(pjt)h(p_{jt})h(pjt​) from equation (11) for punish, minus the inspection cost of equation (12) for inspect), and then the state moves to st+2s_{t+2}st+2​, where the plant chooses again and obtains V(st+2)V(s_{t+2})V(st+2​), discounted by one more round:

W(st+1)=∑aR,t+1Pr⁡(aR,t+1∣st+1){πj(aR,t+1∣st+1)+δ∑st+2f(st+2∣aR,t+1,st+1)V(st+2)}W(s_{t+1})=\sum_{a_{R,t+1}}\Pr(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})\left\{\pi_j(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})+\delta\sum_{s_{t+2}}f(s_{t+2}|a_{R,t+1},s_{t+1})V(s_{t+2})\right\}W(st+1​)=aR,t+1​∑​Pr(aR,t+1​∣st+1​){πj​(aR,t+1​∣st+1​)+δst+2​∑​f(st+2​∣aR,t+1​,st+1​)V(st+2​)}

The weights Pr⁡(aR,t+1∣st+1)\Pr(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})Pr(aR,t+1​∣st+1​) are the machine's logit policy from equation (10), which the plant knows. Substituting WWW into the first line gives the target:

vj(ajt∣st)=πj(ajt∣st)+ej(ajt∣st)+δ∑st+1f(st+1∣ajt,st)∑aR,t+1Pr⁡(aR,t+1∣st+1)×{πj(aR,t+1∣st+1)+δ∑st+2f(st+2∣aR,t+1,st+1)V(st+2)}\begin{aligned} v_j(a_{jt}|s_t)={}&\pi_j(a_{jt}|s_t)+e_j(a_{jt}|s_t)+\delta\sum_{s_{t+1}}f(s_{t+1}|a_{jt},s_t)\sum_{a_{R,t+1}}\Pr(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})\\ &\times\left\{\pi_j(a_{R,t+1}|s_{t+1})+\delta\sum_{s_{t+2}}f(s_{t+2}|a_{R,t+1},s_{t+1})V(s_{t+2})\right\} \end{aligned}vj​(ajt​∣st​)=​πj​(ajt​∣st​)+ej​(ajt​∣st​)+δst+1​∑​f(st+1​∣ajt​,st​)aR,t+1​∑​Pr(aR,t+1​∣st+1​)×{πj​(aR,t+1​∣st+1​)+δst+2​∑​f(st+2​∣aR,t+1​,st+1​)V(st+2​)}​

Here πj(comply∣st)=−k\pi_j(\text{comply}|s_t)=-kπj​(comply∣st​)=−k and πj(ignore∣st)=0\pi_j(\text{ignore}|s_t)=0πj​(ignore∣st​)=0. If the machine accepts, the stage ends and the continuation term inside the braces is zero.

One point is left implicit in the note. The V(st+2)V(s_{t+2})V(st+2​) on the right must be the expected value before the round-(t+2)(t+2)(t+2) shocks are drawn, because those shocks are unknown at ttt. Equation (14) defines the value including the realized shocks, so the object used here is its expectation, which under the type-I extreme value assumption is

V(st+2)=Ee[max⁡a∈APvj(a∣st+2)]=σalog⁡∑a∈APexp⁡(vˉj(a∣st+2)/σa)+σaγEV(s_{t+2})=\mathbb{E}_e\left[\max_{a\in A_P}v_j(a|s_{t+2})\right]=\sigma_a\log\sum_{a\in A_P}\exp\left(\bar{v}_j(a|s_{t+2})/\sigma_a\right)+\sigma_a\gamma_EV(st+2​)=Ee​[a∈AP​max​vj​(a∣st+2​)]=σa​loga∈AP​∑​exp(vˉj​(a∣st+2​)/σa​)+σa​γE​

with γE≈0.577\gamma_E\approx 0.577γE​≈0.577 the Euler constant. With this reading, equation (13) is a recursion in the deterministic values vˉj\bar{v}_jvˉj​ that is solved by backward induction from the last round.

This defines the value of a state at which the plant moves as the value of its best action, where AP={comply,ignore}A_P=\{\text{comply},\text{ignore}\}AP​={comply,ignore} is the plant's action set and vj(ajt∣st)v_j(a_{jt}|s_t)vj​(ajt​∣st​) is the choice-specific value from equation (13). Payoffs are negative or zero (costs of regulation), so maximizing value is the same as minimizing the expected discounted cost of regulation. Because vjv_jvj​ includes the shock ej(ajt∣st)e_j(a_{jt}|s_t)ej​(ajt​∣st​), the maximum is taken after the plant has seen its shocks for the round; Vj(st)V_j(s_t)Vj​(st​) is therefore random from the point of view of earlier rounds and of the econometrician.

What enters the recursion in equation (13) is its expectation over the shocks. With i.i.d. type-I extreme value shocks of scale σa\sigma_aσa​ and vˉj=vj−ej\bar{v}_j=v_j-e_jvˉj​=vj​−ej​, this has the familiar log-sum form

Ee[Vj(st)]=σalog⁡[exp⁡(vˉj(comply∣st)σa)+exp⁡(vˉj(ignore∣st)σa)]+σaγE\mathbb{E}_e\left[V_j(s_t)\right]=\sigma_a\log\left[\exp\left(\frac{\bar{v}_j(\text{comply}|s_t)}{\sigma_a}\right)+\exp\left(\frac{\bar{v}_j(\text{ignore}|s_t)}{\sigma_a}\right)\right]+\sigma_a\gamma_EEe​[Vj​(st​)]=σa​log[exp(σa​vˉj​(comply∣st​)​)+exp(σa​vˉj​(ignore∣st​)​)]+σa​γE​

where γE\gamma_EγE​ is the Euler constant. The expected value exceeds the larger of the two deterministic values: the plant has an option value from being able to pick whichever action has the better shock.

Equations (13) and (14) together are solved by backward induction over rounds, since the round is part of the state and chains end when the machine accepts. The solution gives the logit choice probabilities of equation (15) for estimation, and, evaluated at the first plant move (t=2t=2t=2) for each pollution level, the penalty value function V^0(p)\hat{V}_0(p)V^0​(p) that the targeting stage uses in equations (5) to (7).

By equation (14) the plant picks the action with the highest vj(a∣st)=vˉj(a∣st)+ej(a∣st)v_j(a|s_t)=\bar{v}_j(a|s_t)+e_j(a|s_t)vj​(a∣st​)=vˉj​(a∣st​)+ej​(a∣st​). The model predicts plant jjj's inspections from the targeting rule in equation (9), but the econometrician does not see u1ju_{1j}u1j​, so the prediction must be averaged over its distribution. An unstated assumption: the moment treats the observed count IjI_jIj​ as exactly equal to the rule's value. If realized inspections were a noisy integer draw around the rule (for example Poisson with mean I\mathcal{I}I), then E[Ij2]\mathbb{E}[I_j^2]E[Ij2​] would exceed E[I2]\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{I}^2]E[I2] by the noise variance, and matching this moment would attribute that noise to regulator information.

This is the GMM criterion for the targeting-stage parameters θT={ϕ,β,λ1,λ2,μc,σ1,σ2}\theta_T=\{\phi,\beta,\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_c,\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}θT​={ϕ,β,λ1​,λ2​,μc​,σ1​,σ2​}. The vector g(θT)=[g1′  g2′  ⋯  g7′]g(\theta_T)=[g_1'\;g_2'\;\cdots\;g_7']g(θT​)=[g1′​g2′​⋯g7′​] stacks the sample averages of seven groups of moments: the pollution-equation moments of equation (17); expected inspections and squared inspections, equations (18) and (19); the probability of running and the mean cost conditional on running; and the variance of pollution and its covariance with inspections. Here ggg is written as a row vector, so g W g′g\,W\,g'gWg′ is a scalar quadratic form, the weighted squared distance of the model's predictions from the data. WWW is a positive definite weighting matrix. The estimator is two-step: a first step with a preliminary WWW gives consistent estimates, which are used to estimate the variance of the moments Ω^\hat{\Omega}Ω^, and the second step uses the efficient choice

W=Ω^−1,Ω^=Var⁡^(N g(θT))W=\hat{\Omega}^{-1},\qquad \hat{\Omega}=\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\left(\sqrt{N}\,g(\theta_T)\right)W=Ω^−1,Ω^=Var(N​g(θT​))

Some moments are analytic (equations (18) and (19)) and others are simulated with S=5000S=5000S=5000 draws of the shocks and costs, because the run decision in equation (5) depends on unobservables in a way that has no closed form once V0V_0V0​ is an interpolated function. Simulation inflates the asymptotic variance by a factor of about 1+1/S1+1/S1+1/S, which is negligible here.

In the constrained estimation the same criterion is minimized subject to the optimal-targeting conditions of equation (21). The efficient weighting is what makes the difference in minimized criteria a test statistic:

N[min⁡θT constrainedg W g′−min⁡θTg W g′] ⟶d χ22N\left[\min_{\theta_T\ \text{constrained}}g\,W\,g'-\min_{\theta_T}g\,W\,g'\right]\ \overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\ \chi_2^2N[θT​ constrainedmin​gWg′−θT​min​gWg′] ⟶d​ χ22​

under the null that the regulator targets optimally, with two degrees of freedom for the two independent constraints.

The regulator's problem is to maximize the objective in equation (7) subject to the budget in equation (8). Write A(λ)\mathcal{A}(\lambda)A(λ) for the objective and B(λ)\mathcal{B}(\lambda)B(λ) for the left side of the budget, and form the Lagrangian with multiplier η\etaη:

L(λ,η)=A(λ)−η[B(λ)−N⋅Iˉ]\mathcal{L}(\lambda,\eta)=\mathcal{A}(\lambda)-\eta\left[\mathcal{B}(\lambda)-N\cdot\bar{I}\right]L(λ,η)=A(λ)−η[B(λ)−N⋅Iˉ]

The endogenous choice variables are λ1\lambda_1λ1​ and λ2\lambda_2λ2​ (β\betaβ and ρ\rhoρ are taken as given). Differentiating with respect to each and with respect to η\etaη gives three first-order conditions:

∂A(λ)∂λ1=η ∂B(λ)∂λ1,∂A(λ)∂λ2=η ∂B(λ)∂λ2,B(λ)=N⋅Iˉ\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_1}=\eta\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_1},\qquad \frac{\partial\mathcal{A}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_2}=\eta\,\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}(\lambda)}{\partial\lambda_2},\qquad \mathcal{B}(\lambda)=N\cdot\bar{I}∂λ1​∂A(λ)​=η∂λ1​∂B(λ)​,∂λ2​∂A(λ)​=η∂λ2​∂B(λ)​,B(λ)=N⋅Iˉ

which is the target. The multiplier η\etaη is the shadow value of the budget: the extra abatement from one more inspection. The first two conditions say that an inspection bought by raising λ1\lambda_1λ1​ must yield the same abatement as one bought by raising λ2\lambda_2λ2​. Since η\etaη is not a parameter of the model, eliminate it by dividing the two conditions:

∂A∂λ1⋅∂B∂λ2=∂A∂λ2⋅∂B∂λ1\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}}{\partial\lambda_1}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}}{\partial\lambda_2}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{A}}{\partial\lambda_2}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathcal{B}}{\partial\lambda_1}∂λ1​∂A​⋅∂λ2​∂B​=∂λ2​∂A​⋅∂λ1​∂B​

This equality and the budget are the two independent nonlinear constraints on θT\theta_TθT​ that the three conditions impose, which is why the distance metric test has two degrees of freedom.

The derivatives can be written out under the probit form of equation (9). For the budget, use the closed form from the panel for equation (18), with μj=λ1+Xj′β1+Tj′β2\mu_j=\lambda_1+X_j'\beta_1+T_j'\beta_2μj​=λ1​+Xj′​β1​+Tj′​β2​:

The marginal abatement from an inspection at a given plant is the density of plants at the cost margin, F′\mathcal{F}'F′, times the penalty gap, times the quantity abated. Raising λ1\lambda_1λ1​ adds inspections mainly to plants in the middle of the index (weight φ(zj)\varphi(z_j)φ(zj​)), while raising λ2\lambda_2λ2​ adds them in proportion to current inspections (weight Φ(zj)\Phi(z_j)Φ(zj​)), that is, to the plants observed to be dirtiest. Optimality equates the abatement per inspection of these two ways of spending the budget. These are necessary conditions for an interior optimum; the objective need not be concave in λ\lambdaλ.
